input:
The vapour pressure of acetone at a temperature of 60 °C can be estimated by means of the Antoine equation, which is a widely used correlation that relates vapour pressure to temperature through three fitted constants. The equation takes the form

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

where $P$ is the vapour pressure, $T$ is the temperature in °C, and $A$, $B$ and $C$ are the Antoine constants for the substance concerned. For acetone, the constants are $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664, with the pressure expressed in mmHg and the temperature in °C. Substituting the temperature of 60 °C into the equation leads to an estimated vapour pressure of 115.5 kPa. The Antoine correlation is one of the standard tools of physical property estimation, and it is routinely used in process calculations whenever a measured value is not immediately to hand, because it requires nothing more than the temperature and a set of constants that have been tabulated for a very large number of common substances. It is important to note that the Antoine constants are valid only over the temperature range over which they were fitted, and that a temperature of 60 °C falling outside that range would leave the estimate without the support of the underlying data. Furthermore, the value obtained from the correlation is only an estimate, and for design purposes the value given in the source databank should be regarded as the governing value in place of the correlation estimate of 115.5 kPa, because it is the databank value that ultimately controls the design.
target:
The vapour pressure of acetone at 60 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

where $P$ is the vapour pressure, $T$ is the temperature in °C, and $A$, $B$ and $C$ are fitted constants. For acetone $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664, with pressure in mmHg and temperature in °C. Substitution of $T$ = 60 °C in the Antoine equation gives an estimate of 115.5 kPa. The constants hold only over their fitted temperature range. The estimate stands only where 60 °C lies inside that range; outside the range the correlation is an extrapolation and the result carries no support from the fit. The three constants are not interchangeable. The subtracted term carries the temperature dependence of the vapour pressure, the constant added to the temperature inside that term shifts the curve along the temperature axis, and the leading constant sets the level of the curve as a whole; a change in any one of them changes the estimate at every temperature, not only at the temperature of interest. The estimate is also stated on a different pressure basis from the constants: the constants take the pressure in mmHg, and the reported estimate is in kPa, so the figure as reported stands on the SI basis on which a design calculation is made. The estimate is a correlation value rather than a measured one. The source databank value governs design, and where the estimate and the databank value differ, the databank value is used and the difference is charged to the correlation. Acetone is therefore assigned 115.5 kPa provisionally: the number is adequate for screening calculations that tolerate correlation error, and it is replaced by the databank value at the point where the design is fixed.
